content: 1. The safety profile of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) indicates they are safe for use during pregnancy and breastfeeding, as well as in older adolescents (15–19 years) and infants. Clinical trials involving single and repeated administration of anti-HIV-1 antibody combinations have shown good tolerability with minimal adverse events, including studies conducted in neonates. 2. For products targeting bacterial or viral pathogens, a short-term safety study in one animal species (justified by the sponsor) may suffice, as per ICH S6 guidelines. Additional toxicity studies, including reproductive toxicity, are not required. When animal disease models are used for proof-of-concept evaluations, safety assessments can provide insights into potential target-associated safety concerns. If this is not feasible, appropriate risk mitigation strategies should be implemented during clinical trials. 3. Efficacy trials for HIV prevention products should adhere to regulatory standards and ethical guidelines, such as those outlined by UNAIDS/WHO. Developers should aim to demonstrate non-inferiority or superiority compared to current standards of care, while acknowledging logistical and cost challenges in conducting such trials. Trial designs should be discussed with ethical and regulatory stakeholders, including national regulatory agencies, and alternative designs may be necessary to evaluate specific agents in the context of evolving prevention standards. 4. WHO guidelines on the quality, safety, and efficacy of biotherapeutic protein products prepared using recombinant DNA technology should be followed. Programmatic benefits, such as less frequent administration, improved safety, and cost-effectiveness, should be considered alongside efficacy. Long-term follow-up studies and post-introduction surveillance are essential to evaluate sustained protection and repeated use. Broad protection across diverse geographies is critical for sustained use. 5. Specimens collected during efficacy trials should support the identification of correlates of risk/protection and breakthrough virus sequencing. Population-level data will help determine whether resistance to specific antibodies emerges over time. Transplacental and breast milk transfer should be considered in product development, and mAb combinations may need to be tailored to regional strain prevalence. 6. If a correlate of neutralization titre is established and accepted by regulators, it could support alternative study designs for next-generation products. For example, a bispecific antibody targeting the human CD4 receptor and HIV-1 Env MPER has demonstrated 100% neutralization of circulating HIV-1 strains in a multiclade panel of 118 viruses. 7. Preferred product characteristics for mAbs include stability under refrigerated conditions (2–8°C) for 2–3 years, with room-temperature lyophilized formulations being potentially advantageous. Ready-to-use formats are preferred for ease of implementation. WHO prequalification can facilitate licensing in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and enable procurement through global mechanisms. 8. Fixed, non-weight-based dosing is preferred, with age-appropriate adjustments for adolescents, adults, infants, and neonates. Co-formulation of mAb combinations is also preferred. Less frequent administration may be advantageous, but further evidence is needed to assess preferences and benefits of longer-duration products. Pharmacokinetic studies should confirm sufficient half-life to support the dosing schedule. 9. Concomitant administration of mAbs for HIV prevention is not expected to interfere with immune responses to non-HIV vaccines. 10. Intravenous (IV) administration is not broadly suitable for programmatic implementation in LMICs, though it may be appropriate in specific settings. Subcutaneous administration is preferred, and best practices for IV administration should be followed if used. 11. WHO is drafting guidance on the manufacture, quality control, and regulatory considerations for mAbs and mAb fragments for infectious diseases. These documents will be accessible on the WHO website once available. 12. Ongoing HIV vaccine and prevention trials are exploring various approaches, including long-acting antiretrovirals, mAbs, and combination products. These trials aim to improve safety, efficacy, and acceptability while addressing the diverse needs of populations at risk for HIV. 13. Aligning dosing schedules with other care-seeking time points, such as injectable contraceptives or infant follow-up visits, may enhance acceptability and adherence. 14. Understanding the preferences and needs of local decision-makers and end-users is critical for successful implementation. Programmatic attributes, such as extended protection duration and tolerability, can reduce delivery costs and improve real-world effectiveness. 15. WHO prequalification and reliance mechanisms can support broad registration and procurement of HIV prevention products, particularly in LMIC settings.
